parties:
Al-haj Md. Shainsuf Haque
Vs.
The Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, and another
full_judgment:
Md. Awlad Ali, J: This supplementary affidavit filed by the appellant-petitioner do form part of the application under section 14 of the Limitation Act. 

 2. On an application under section 14 of the Limitation Act rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the delay of 52 days, which now stands at 28 days according to the correct calculation, in filing the Customs Appeal No. 14 of 2001 should not be condoned. 

 6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, has contended that the petitioner having prosecuted the proceeding in the writ court with due diligence and having persued the matter for same remedy in good faith and the proceeding before the writ court being a Civil Proceeding, the petitioner is entitled to the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act read with section 29 of the same Act. He has pointed out that the writ petition was filed on 16.4.2001 and thus the petitioner spent 29 days a wrong forum which shall be excluded in computing the period of limitation in preferring the appeal under section 196(D) of the Customs Act. 

 7. It appears that the appeal was presented before this court on 20.5.2001. The impugned order was passed by the Tribunal on 29.1.2001, and the petitioner received the copy of the impugned order sometime after the date on which it was sent to him, and the order was sent to the petitioner on 22.2.2001. According to the provision of section 196D, sixty days limitation shall be computing from the date when the notice of the impugned order is served upon the petitioner. Accordingly 60 days expired on 22.4.2001, and consequently there has been delay of 28. days in preferring the appeal. Now the question arises whether the period from 16.4.2001 to 14.5.2001 shall be excluded in computing the period of limitation in preferring the appeal before this court. In order that section 14 of the Limitation Act may apply the person claiming the benefit of it must fulfill certain conditions, vi z- 

 9. As regards the application of section 14 of the Limitation Act Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has contended that although the Customs Act is a special law and the tithe in preferring appeal is prescribed therein but the application of the provision of section 14 of the Limitation Act has not been expressly excluded by the Customs Act 1969. In this regard section 29 of the Limitation act is also relevant. Section 29 of the Limitation Act provides as follows: 

 (2) where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, 'appeal or application, a. period, of limitation different from the .period prescribed thereto by the First Schedule, the provision of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefore ,in that schedule, and  for  the purpose of determining. any period of limitation 'prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law- 

 Pointing out the above provision of law Mr. Bhuiyan has submitted that section 14 of the Limitation Act has not been expressly excluded by the Customs Act. In plain reading of sub-section 2(a) it will be seen that sufficient indication is available to the effect that unless the application of sub-section 2 clause (a) is expressly excluded by a special law the applicability of the section in computing the period of limitation the provision of section 14 can be invoked provided the conditions as stated above are fulfilled. The period spent in a Civil proceeding in a court shall be excluded in computing the period of limitation. Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to us the case of Bangladesh Bank and others Versus Mohd. Abdul Mannan reported in 40 DLR (AD) 1. In para 5 of the cited case it has been observed by the Appellate Division that before considering whether the provision in section 14 are expressly excluded by the Administrative Tribunal Act it should be seen whether the previous proceeding (the Writ Petition) before the High Court Division was started in good faith. The appellant-bank which was respondent before the Tribunal did not say that the proceeding under Writ jurisdiction was not taken by the employee in good faith but was taken for the purpose of killing time. Although the applicability of section 14 was not finally decided in that cage since the point of limitation was not urged before the Administrative Tribunal, but indication is there that if the previous proceeding is started and prosecuted with due diligence and in good faith, section 14 of the Limitation Act may be attracted. Reference has also been made to the case of Syed Amid Hossain Vs. Mrs. Nadera Rahman reported in 5 BLD(AD) 317 where referring to section 14 and 29(2) of the Limitation Act, it has been stated that moot point is whether application of section 14 is barred by section 29(2). Section 32(3) of the Waqf Ordinance is undisputedly a special law within the meaning of section 29(2) as quoted above and this law prescribed a limitation different from the prescribed by the Limitation Act and the period of limitation as to revision is 90 days which has obviously long expired. Only section 14 may save this revision. Section 29(2) does not say that section 14, like section 4, 9 to 19 is excluded in all cases governed by the special Law; rather it says that these sections are applicable, but only "in so far as they are not expressly excluded” by the special law. In other words, unless application of these sections is not excluded in express words and language, they shall apply. 

 10. Mr. S.A. M. Mahbub Elahi, the learned Deputy Attorney General, has contended that since time limit has been prescribed under section 196D of the Customs Act which is a special law the time spent in previous proceeding can not be excluded in view of the provision of section 14 of the Limitation Act. He has referred to a decision in the case of Md. Abdus Sukkur-Versus-Chairman, National Board of Revenue and others reported in 17 BLD(AD)4 where Administrative Tribunal held that the petitioner filed various Tribunal cases before filing the present tribunal case and as such he will get the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal repelled this contention and held that section of the Limitation Act is not applicable to proceedings before the Tribunal. The Appellate Division held that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal correctly decided the point. The Administrative Tribunal does not make any provision for application of section 14 of the Limitation Act in a proceeding before the Administrative Tribunal, section 14 is not applicable. Since the Administrative Tribunal is not a court as contemplated under section 14 of the Limitation Act, section 14 of the Limitation Act is not attracted and not apply. The other case as has been cited by the learned D.A.G. is the Commissioner of Sales Tax Uttar Prodesh Luchnow =versus= M/s. Parson Tools and Plants, Kanpur reported in A.I.R. 1975 (SC) 1039 where it has been decided that the appellate authority and the Judge (Revisions) under the U.P. Sales Tax are not courts but merely administrative Tribunal sections 14(2) of the Limitation Act does not in terms apply to proceeding before them. 

 11. The relief as sought under section 14 of the Limitation Act is according to the language as employed in that section is not for condonation of delay, it is for exclusion of the time spent in a wrong forum. Under Section 14 of the Limitation Act the court cannot exercise its discretionary power to condone the delay or extend the time for preferring the application or appeal as the court can do under section 5 of the Act on being satisfied on the cause shown. If on fact it is found that the litigant party has acted in good faith and persued the same remedy in a wrong forum with due diligence, the court shall exclude the time in computing the period of limitation. It appears that the petitioner had spent 29 days in writ forum including 16.4.2001 and 14.5.2001, and there has been delay of 28 days, reckoning the days from the date upon which the petitioner was served with notice of the order passed by the Tribunal. If 29 days spent in the writ court is excluded according to the provision of section 14 read with section 29 as referred to above, the appeal is very much within 60 days as prescribed under section 196D of the Customs Act. Accordingly the delay of 28 days is excluded in preferring the Appeal.
